Lothe
lōth
v. (the Authorized Version's spelling of loathe: to abhor, to turn from with disgust)
Saxon lathian, to be hateful. The seventeenth-century spelling drops the second a. Three of its four occurrences are Ezekiel's, and in every one of those the object of the loathing is the sinner's own self.

Biblical Definition

Ezekiel uses this word for something the modern church has almost entirely lost: the self-abhorrence that follows restoring grace. Not before it — after it. “And they that escape of you shall remember me among the nations whither they shall be carried captives… and they shall lothe themselves for the evils which they have committed in all their abominations” (Eze 6:9). Again: “there shall ye remember your ways… and ye shall lothe yourselves in your own sight for all your evils that ye have committed” (Eze 20:43). And most pointedly in the great new-covenant chapter, immediately after God promises the new heart, the new spirit and His own Spirit put within them: “Then shall ye remember your own evil ways… and shall lothe yourselves in your own sight for your iniquities and for your abominations” (Eze 36:31). The order is decisive. God cleanses, gives the new heart, causes them to walk in His statutes — and then they loathe themselves. This is not the despair of the unforgiven; it is the grief of the pardoned, and it deepens rather than diminishes as grace advances. The fourth occurrence is the plainest possible use: after the first plague “the Egyptians shall lothe to drink of the water of the river” (Exo 7:18).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines loathe as to feel disgust at any thing; to have an extreme aversion of the appetite to food or drink; and figuratively, to hate, to abhor.

expand to see more

LOATHE, v.t. To feel disgust at any thing; to have an extreme aversion of the appetite to food or drink.

1. To hate; to dislike greatly; to abhor. Ye shall loathe yourselves in your own sight. Ezekiel 20.

LOATHING, n. Extreme disgust; abhorrence.

ABHOR, v.t. To hate extremely, or with contempt; to loathe, detest or abominate.

Key Scripture

Eze 36:31 — "Then shall ye remember your own evil ways, and your doings that were not good, and shall lothe yourselves in your own sight for your iniquities and for your abominations."

Eze 20:43 — "And there shall ye remember your ways, and all your doings, wherein ye have been defiled; and ye shall lothe yourselves in your own sight for all your evils that ye have committed."

Eze 6:9 — "And they that escape of you shall remember me among the nations whither they shall be carried captives, because I am broken with their whorish heart, which hath departed from me, and with their eyes, which go a whoring after their idols: and they shall lothe themselves for the evils which they have committed in all their abominations."

Exo 7:18 — "And the fish that is in the river shall die, and the river shall stink; and the Egyptians shall lothe to drink of the water of the river."

Modern Corruption

Self-loathing is treated as a pathology to be cured; Ezekiel makes it the fruit of the new heart, not its absence.

expand to see more

The therapeutic reading of these verses is that they describe an unhealthy self-image, and the counsel given is to replace loathing with self-acceptance. Ezekiel 36 forbids the reading by its own sequence. God says He will sprinkle clean water, give a new heart, take away the stony heart, put His Spirit within them, cause them to walk in His statutes — and only then, then shall ye remember… and shall lothe yourselves. The abhorrence is the effect of grace already received. It is what a forgiven man feels when he sees, in the light of the mercy that saved him, what he actually was and did.

This must be distinguished with care from two counterfeits. It is not the despair of Judas, which had no hope in it and ended in a rope; godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation, and the sorrow of the world worketh death. And it is not the modern self-hatred that is really wounded pride, a man furious at himself for not being what he wished to be. Ezekiel's loathing is directed at sin against God, held by a man who knows he is pardoned, and it produces worship rather than paralysis. The Puritans knew this territory better than we do, and they were not morbid men; they were the freest.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qut (H6962), to loathe, to feel a loathing at; la'ah (H3811), to be weary or disgusted; shiqquts (H8251), abomination, detestable thing.

expand to see more

Hebrew qut (H6962) — to loathe, to be grieved with, to feel a loathing; Ezekiel 6:9, 20:43, 36:31, always of loathing oneself.

Hebrew la'ah (H3811) — to be weary, to be disgusted with; Exodus 7:18, the Egyptians loathed to drink.

Hebrew to'ebah (H8441) — abomination, that which is detestable to God; the object of the loathing in Ezekiel 36:31.

Hebrew leb chadash (H3820, H2319) — a new heart; Ezekiel 36:26, given before the loathing of verse 31.

Greek metanoia (G3341) — a change of mind, repentance; 2 Corinthians 7:10, godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation.

Usage

"“Ye shall lothe yourselves in your own sight” — after the new heart, not before."

"“They shall lothe themselves for the evils which they have committed”."

"“The Egyptians shall lothe to drink” — the plainest sense of the word."
